evidence: Pause at each page and invite students to say out loud what the sun sees on each page and add it to the What the Sun Sees anchor chart.
rationale: Students share relevant and accurate information about what the sun "sees" through multiple activities: they say aloud what the sun sees on each page of the text ("invite students to say out loud what the sun sees on each page"), they turn and talk with partners about photographs and videos ("'What could the sun "see" or observe?' (an elephant walking through a forest or jungle)"), and they role-play scenes. These activities meet the relevant-information and accurate-information clauses. However, the "variety of different modes" clause is only partially met: students communicate almost exclusively through oral speech (whole-group, partner talk, role-play). The lesson mentions optional whiteboards for scaffolding active viewing, not as a distinct sharing mode, and no written, drawn, or digital sharing mode is used by students to share information. The variety-of-modes component is therefore thin, capping the overall alignment at partial.

evidence: 'What is one connection you made during the Interactive Word Wall protocol?' (Responses will vary.)
rationale: The lesson partially meets the standard's interpretation (I) clauses. Students exercise comprehension skills by making vocabulary connections during the Interactive Word Wall protocol ("'What is one connection you made during the Interactive Word Wall protocol?'"), by describing what the sun "sees" using evidence from illustrations, photographs, and videos ("'What could the sun 'see' or observe?'"), and by role-playing sections of the text to demonstrate understanding. However, the composition (C) clauses are not met: no student construction of text occurs in this lesson — the teacher only previews that students "will use these observations to write a narrative poem … beginning in the next lesson." Additionally, the repertoire built is narrow (vocabulary connections and observation/description), not a broad draw across multiple comprehension strategies, capping the comprehension clauses at partially met.

evidence: 'What is one connection you made during the Interactive Word Wall protocol?' (Responses will vary.)
rationale: The standard decomposes into four clauses joined by commas (an OR-like list of collaborative purposes under one "work with others" act): discuss topics, investigate questions, solve problems, and explore and create texts. Students discuss topics collaboratively during the Interactive Word Wall protocol in small groups ("What is one connection you made during the Interactive Word Wall protocol?") and during turn-and-talk about photographs/videos. Students investigate questions collaboratively when they turn and talk with elbow partners to answer "What could the sun 'see' or observe?" using photographs and video evidence. Students explore the text collaboratively through the Role-Play protocol ("Invite students to begin role-playing the following sections of text"), but no text creation occurs in this lesson — the teacher states creation will begin "in the next lesson," so the "create texts" component of that clause is unmet, making it partially met. No problem-solving activity is present. With three of four purpose-clauses at least partially met, alignment is partial.

evidence: 'What if we remove the words crowded, bustling, and noisy? I'll give you time to think and discuss with a partner.'
rationale: The lesson touches descriptive words (adjectives) in the read-aloud text and engages students in related activities, but the core cognitive work of identifying and explaining is largely teacher-performed. The teacher "point[s] out that it is being used as an adjective because it describes what the barnyard looks like" for each word (crowded, bustling, noisy), doing the identifying and explaining. Students are directed to think about what happens when adjectives are removed ("What if we remove the words crowded, bustling, and noisy? I'll give you time to think and discuss with a partner") and to find connections between adjective sets ("Can you figure out the connection between these adjectives and the adjectives quiet, empty, and silent?"), which partially engages them in recognizing and reasoning about descriptive words. Both clauses are partially met because the student acts are thin proxies — the teacher performs the explicit identification and explanation while students engage with adjacent tasks (noticing removal effects, making word connections) rather than directly identifying descriptive words in the text or explaining their use.
standard_raw_text: Identify and explain the use of descriptive words in texts. (I)

rationale: The consume clause is partially met: students engage with multiple modalities — a printed picture book read aloud (pages 1–16), displayed photographs (day photograph 1, day photograph 2), and video clips ("British Wildlife Filmed on a DSLR," "Street Time Lapse") — and respond orally ("What could the sun 'see' or observe?"). However, the lesson never asks students to analyze or attend to how different genres, text features, or craft techniques are integrated across these modes; consumption of multiple modes occurs but without the integration/craft awareness the standard names. The produce clause is not met: no student production of a multimodal text occurs in this lesson; the teacher only previews that students "will use these observations to write a narrative poem … beginning in the next lesson," so the construction act is deferred entirely.
